title: HTTP Services Over Encrypted Overlay
description: Run standard HTTP services over Pilot Protocol's encrypted overlay. Call an agent's API from Go or through the optional gateway.
seoTitle: HTTP Services Over Encrypted Overlay | Pilot Protocol Blog
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: Every HTTP library in every language works with TCP sockets. Pilot Protocol speaks UDP. You might assume these are incompatible. They are not. Pilot's driver implements
server and client work over Pilot connections without modification. You write a normal HTTP handler, listen on a Pilot port, and the bytes travel over an encrypted UDP tunnel through NAT. Standard
calls can reach the same services through the optional gateway, a separate binary that needs root.

This tutorial builds from a single HTTP endpoint to a three-service REST API mesh running entirely over the encrypted overlay. By the end, you will have agents exposing HTTP services that any standard client can consume, with

Pilot's virtual port space is separate from the OS port space. Port 80 on Pilot does not conflict with port 80 on your machine. Gateway: Bridge to Standard HTTP Clients
The Go driver approach works for agent-to-agent communication. But what about external tools --
call, or a browser? The Pilot gateway bridges the overlay network to your local machine.
The gateway is a separate, optional binary.

runs it in the foreground. It needs root, because it adds loopback aliases.

fields.code:
# Map Agent A's address to a local IP and expose port 80
sudo pilotctl extras gateway start --ports 80 0:0000.0002.0003

# The gateway assigns loopback aliases from 10.4.0.0/16, starting at 10.4.0.1
# Stop it with Ctrl-C, or: sudo pkill -TERM pilot-gateway

children.text: Incoming TCP connections are forwarded over the encrypted Pilot tunnel to the agent's port 80. Responses come back the same way.
Now any standard HTTP client works:

fields.code:
# curl works
curl http://10.4.0.1/api/status
{"status":"healthy","agent":"0:0000.0002.0003","version":"1.0.0"}

# Python requests works
python3 -c "import requests; print(requests.get('http://10.4.0.1/api/status').json())"

# Even browsers work (navigate to http://10.4.0.1/api/status)

children.text: No TLS needed on the client side.

The gateway accepts plain HTTP on the local loopback. The traffic is encrypted at the Pilot tunnel layer (AES-256-GCM) before it leaves your machine. The client does not need certificates, and there is no certificate hostname mismatch to deal with.

Now for the real use case. Three agents running microservices: Users, Orders, and Inventory. Each exposes a REST API on Pilot port 80. The gateway makes them all accessible as local services.
Start one gateway with mappings for all three agents:

fields.code:
# Map each service to a local IP
sudo pilotctl extras gateway start --ports 80 \
    0:0000.0002.0001 0:0000.0002.0002 0:0000.0002.0003
# Users -> 10.4.0.1, Orders -> 10.4.0.2, Inventory -> 10.4.0.3

children.text: Now query the services with standard HTTP tools:

fields.code:
# Get all users
curl http://10.4.0.1/api/users
[{"id":"u1","name":"Alice","email":"alice@example.com"},{"id":"u2","name":"Bob","email":"bob@example.com"}]

# Get orders for user u1
curl "http://10.4.0.2/api/orders?user_id=u1"
[{"id":"o1","user_id":"u1","item":"GPU Cluster Hours","total":250,"status":"completed"},{"id":"o3","user_id":"u1","item":"Model Training Run","total":1200,"status":"active"}]

# Check inventory for a SKU
curl "http://10.4.0.3/api/inventory/check?sku=gpu-a100"
{"sku":"gpu-a100","available":true,"count":48}

children.text: These are standard HTTP requests to local IP addresses. The encryption, NAT traversal, and peer authentication all happen transparently at the Pilot tunnel layer. Your Python script, your JavaScript frontend, your Go microservice -- they all use their native HTTP clients unchanged.
The services can also call each other. The Orders service can look up user details by dialing the Users service through Pilot:
The mesh works the same way whether all three agents are on the same machine, on different machines in the same datacenter, or on different continents behind different NATs. The code does not change.
Port 443: Current Behavior and Secure-Layer Roadmap

Today, Pilot ports 80 and 443 both ride the same AES-256-GCM encrypted tunnel. Port 443 is the secure-service convention; it does not yet add a second per-connection encryption layer in the shipping SDK.
A per-connection secure layer exists as a Go package,
in a channel with its own ephemeral X25519 key and AES-256-GCM. The driver does
in the current Go SDK, and listening on port 443 rides the same tunnel encryption as port 80. The code below uses the shipping
A second layer derives a separate key for each logical connection, adding isolation beyond the peer-specific tunnel secret. With today's driver you only get it by wrapping the connection yourself.
This is the same defense-in-depth approach as running TLS inside a VPN tunnel. It protects against key compromise at any single layer.

The gateway also supports secure ports:

fields.code:
# Gateway with secure port mapping
sudo pilotctl extras gateway start --ports 443 0:0000.0002.0003

# Access via curl (still plain HTTP on the local side)

children.text: The gateway terminates the Pilot tunnel encryption and serves plain HTTP locally. Data in transit between agents is protected by the tunnel layer today; operators should still assess the local segment and host boundary for their environment.
The HTTP ecosystem is enormous. Decades of tools, libraries, frameworks, middleware, and monitoring solutions all speak HTTP. By making Pilot connections compatible with

The encryption is automatic. The NAT traversal is automatic. The peer authentication is automatic. You write HTTP handlers and they just work, whether your agents are on the same LAN or on different continents behind symmetric NAT.
